final_proof:
We use the following standard consequence of Ingham's prime-gap theorem. Ingham proved that there are constants C>0 and x_0 such that, whenever p<q are consecutive primes and p>=x_0, one has q-p <= C p^{5/8}. Consequently, there is an integer M such that for every integer m>=M there is a prime q satisfying

  m^3<q and q+1<(m+1)^3.                                      (1)

Indeed, enlarge M so that the largest prime p not exceeding m^3 is at least x_0 whenever m>=M, and so that

  C m^{15/8}+1<3m^2+3m+1=(m+1)^3-m^3.

Such an M exists because 15/8<2; the first requirement is possible because the primes are unbounded. Let p be the largest prime at most m^3 and let q be the next prime. These are consecutive primes, q>m^3, and Ingham's estimate gives

  q <= p+C p^{5/8} <= m^3+C m^{15/8}.

The displayed choice of M therefore gives q+1<(m+1)^3, proving (1).

Choose a prime a_1>=M; one exists by Euclid's theorem. Having chosen the prime a_n, apply (1) with m=a_n and choose a prime a_{n+1} such that

  a_n^3<a_{n+1} and a_{n+1}+1<(a_n+1)^3.                       (2)

This recursively defines primes a_n for all n>=1. Notice that a_{n+1}>a_n^3>a_n, so every a_n remains at least M and the recursion is valid.

For n>=1 define the closed interval

  J_n=[l_n,u_n]=[a_n^{1/3^n}, (a_n+1)^{1/3^n}].

Since all quantities are positive, taking 3^{n+1}-st roots in (2) preserves the strict inequalities and yields

  l_n=(a_n^3)^{1/3^{n+1}}<a_{n+1}^{1/3^{n+1}}=l_{n+1}

and

  u_{n+1}=(a_{n+1}+1)^{1/3^{n+1}}<((a_n+1)^3)^{1/3^{n+1}}=u_n.

Thus J_{n+1} is contained in the interior of J_n for every n. By completeness of the real numbers these nested nonempty compact intervals have a common point. Explicitly, let A=sup{l_n:n>=1}. For each fixed n, u_n is an upper bound for every l_k: if k<=n then l_k<=l_n<=u_n, while if k>=n then l_k<=u_k<=u_n. Hence l_n<=A<=u_n, so A belongs to every J_n. Moreover, because A belongs to J_{n+1} and J_{n+1} is contained in the interior of J_n, we actually have

  l_n<A<u_n

for every n>=1. Raising this inequality to the positive integer power 3^n gives

  a_n<A^{3^n}<a_n+1.

Therefore floor(A^{3^n})=a_n. Since a_n is prime for every n>=1, this real number A has the required property.
